title: Laborem Exercens (1981)
hookLine: John Paul II: work is for the person, not the person for work

cards: A field of grain on a sabbath. Jesus's disciples are hungry, and as they walk they pluck the heads of grain. Critics object: that's work, and it's the day of rest.
In Mark's Gospel, Jesus flips the order. In the Douay-Rheims: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." The rule serves the person.

This path met the heart of John Paul the Second's letter on human work with the carpenter of Nazareth. Today, the rest of that letter, Laborem Exercens, which makes the same flip about the job you go to on Monday.
Work is for the person, not the person for work.

teach.b: First, people before capital. Laborem Exercens says work has priority over capital: the money, machines, buildings and tools of a business. All of these are things, and things are meant to serve persons.
The twist: the machines themselves are the fruit of earlier human work, the inheritance of generations of workers. Capital is work, piled up. So it makes no sense to let the pile rule the people.
Second, the boss behind the boss.

John Paul the Second distinguishes a direct employer, the one who signs your contract, from what he calls an indirect employer: the laws, governments, markets and international arrangements that shape what any direct employer can offer.
Whether work treats people well depends on that whole web, not just on a kind manager. Third, the tiredness. The letter doesn't pretend work is always joyful.
It's honest about sweat and toil. And it offers Christians a way to carry that: work as a share in God's activity as creator, and its hardness, borne patiently, as a share in Christ's cross.
Not a reason to accept unjust conditions. A way to find meaning inside honest, hard days. Fourth, Monday.

teach.h: THE SABBATH WAS MADE FOR MAN.
teach.b: If work is for the person, then a person crushed by work has the order upside down, like a sabbath that starves the hungry. The person comes first: before the target, before the inbox, before the machine.

how: Catholics often draw on Laborem Exercens in labor ministry, in Catholic business ethics and in keeping Sunday as a day of rest, and the letter is a standard text in Catholic teaching on work.

games.q: you run a workshop. new machines could make more if your people worked longer, faster, with fewer breaks. what does Laborem Exercens put first?
o: the machines: they cost the most.
the output: work is measured by what it makes.
the people: work is for the person.
games.why: the letter gives work priority over capital. the machines are themselves the fruit of earlier work, and things exist to serve persons.

practice: For a moment, no task, no list, no planning tomorrow: notice where work lives in your body, the jaw, the shoulders, the eyes, the hands, and let each one go a little, in turn.

If thoughts of what's undone arrive, let them stand outside the door; you are not a machine on pause, you are a person resting. If you pray, rest before God the way the sabbath invites; if you don't, simply rest.

wordCard.voice: Laborem Exercens. John Paul the Second's letter on human work: people before capital, a whole web of employers, and work made for the person. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: doing work, or exercising labor, the letter's opening words.

carryVoice: Your line: the person first. Capital is only work, piled up. See you tomorrow.
